speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Kaplan that Bill C-9, an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to enact an Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have an opportunity to speak against Bill C-9. It is quite a bad Bill although admittedly it is not as bad as Bill C-157 which went before it. Rather, it looks as if Bill C-157 was made as bad as possible in order to make Bill C-9 look good.
Bill C-9 does three things. First of all, it threatens Canadians who dissent from the Government, Canadians who support change in Canada and Canadians who support peace and justice in the world. All are threatened with practically uncontrolled mail opening and government action to infiltrate and disrupt their organizations by secret operatives. The Bill also authorizes the Canadian Security Intelligence Service to become secretly obligated to unnamed foreign governments. As a counterpart of that, it excludes elected Members of Parliament and, for that matter, non-elected members of the Senate, from reviewing its work in any thorough way. It even excludes the appointed review committee from reviewing Cabinet documents.
The background of this Bill is very important. It was pointed out just a few years ago by a person who has done more to defend the liberty of Canadians than the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan)-I refer to Jean-Claude Parrot, the head of the postal workers' union-that in Canada we seem to have two kinds of laws. When the postal workers go out on legal strike, the Government passes a law to make the strike illegal. When the RCMP open letters illegally, the Government passes a law to make it legal.
This is what this Bill is all about, Mr. Speaker. In the past it was the unions which were attacked, unions being second-class citizens. Union members are the only ones who can be sent to jail for not working. Professional people are now being attacked. In the 1960s the approach of the Government was more soft sell. It tried to fund the dissenters in order to take over dissent. By the end of the 1960s the professional people who dissented felt, in the words of George Grant, a well-known conservative philosopher, that dissent had become bureaucratized, that the dissenters had been co-opted. Around 1970, with the burning down of the Praxis Building in Toronto, tougher tactics began to emerge, not only the burning of the Praxis Building but burning a barn, defaming left leaders, forging documents, and all kinds of notorious, dirty tricks. There was some success achieved, I suppose, in the disruption of dissent and criticism during the 1970s by those means. Those tactics were not used, so far as can be determined, against espionage or sabotage. They were used against what might have vaguely been defined as subversion. But no criminal charges were laid in connection with incidents which would be commonly understood to be criminal activities engaged in by the police.
Following public outcry and considerable condemnation from the McDonald Commission, there were many crimes by the RCMP documented. There was no prosecution for these crimes outside the Province of Quebec. There has been no identified disciplinary action. We are told some people have been disciplined. We do not know whether they were disciplined for the crimes they committed or disciplined for helping to expose the crimes. There has been no undertaking that those crimes would cease. In fact, the effect of Bill C-157 and its "child" tends not to make those crimes punishable but to illegalize or intimidate dissent and criticism.
The Government proceeded as follows: after the report of the McDonald Commission of 1981, it delayed for two years and would take no action on any of the recommendations. On the question of prosecution it made sure it delayed until the statute of limitations rescued it. The Government then put forward Bill C-157, an amazingly bad Bill which brought unanimity from coast to coast among the provincial attorneys general in condemning the Bill. That was a remarkable achievement, Mr. Speaker.
The Bill was then diverted to the Senate for hearings where it was felt it would get more sympathetic treatment than in Parliament since there is no third party opposition in the Senate. The Senate committee under Senator Pitfield made certain recommendations which were not as strong as the recommendations of the McDonald Commission and tended to

mask and hide the McDonald Commission recommendations from public attention.
The Government now, after this delay, has asked us to move suddenly on this Bill. It was even introduced on a Friday with less than one day's notice. The Friday before a Minister and his assistant whined about the fact that we were debating fisheries on a Friday-an important subject-although it was the Government which gave only one day's notice that it would be an Opposition Day. The Government then tried to slide Bill C-9 through about 10 days ago, on a Friday, hoping that it would move right through to committee without any serious debate on second reading.
The faults of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, are, first of all, that intrusion threatens Canadian dissenters with very vague language. The Bill refers to "any action directed toward or intended ultimately to lead to the destruction or overthrow". That allows any policeman or any civilian-type investigator the scope to be able to say: "I think I need to investigate that fellow. Some day he might be doing something which would tend to lead to the overthrow of the government".
[DOT] (ms)
By contrast, Mr. Speaker, the United States, which has much more serious experience with real espionage and terrorism, introduced new guidelines a year ago in which domestic security and terrorism investigation may be initiated "when the facts or circumstances reasonably indicate that two or more persons are engaged in an enterprise for the purpose of furthering political or social goals wholly or in part through activities that involve force or violence and a violation of the criminal laws of the United States". There must be much more specific evidence before they are allowed to proceed with that kind of an investigation. They must be able to show the magnitude of the threatened harm, the likelihood that it will occur, the immediacy of the threat-not some ultimate, "some day, maybe" action; it must be something immediate.
What is strikingly absent from this proposed Bill is that they must show that danger to privacy and free expression are sufficient to warrant an investigation. The Canadian law is much weaker in protecting Canadians. In spite of the recommendations of the McDonald Commission, or even of the friendly Pitfield committee, Bill C-9 excludes any mention of the duty of the secret service to convince the judge that the investigation is really needed. That is to say, that the damage to privacy is outweighed by the possible immediate damage if the investigation is not carried forward. That was asked for by both commissions and notably excluded in the Solicitor General's Bill.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, intrusions such as mail opening with no more control that in the past, infiltration and disruption, threaten Canadians who are advocating social change at home or peace and international justice. For example, people who criticized the World Bank loan to South Africa could be caught in this kind of a coil. On the other hand, people who support the African National Congress would likewise be caught. Or even people who support the World Bank loan to
South Africa, considering that country is engaged in violating international law by using that money to finance its war against Namibia, could be caught by this vague wording.
Canadians who support the FDR-FMLN resistance to the fascist government in El Salvador could be caught under this law. Likewise, Canadians who support D'Aubisson, the architect of mass violence and the probable architect of the murder of an archbishop, could be caught under this law. Supporters of the dictator Pinochet could be caught, or opponents as well. The law is meaningless. In the case of Chile, it would even catch the Roman Catholic church. Supporters of Baby Doc Duvalier in Haiti, that is to say, people carrying on CIDA projects, could be caught under this law. People carrying on CIDA projects in Honduras could be suspected of supporting a country which is a military base for the United States to invade and intimidate neighbouring nations in Central America.
By the way, aliens are given slightly more rights under this proposed law but not substantially more. However this part is not in keeping with the statement of the former Minister of Immigration who said that a mark of a civilized country is how it treats the poorest of its people. He suggests an equal test is how a civilized country treats those who are not its citizens and find themselves in desperate circumstances. These are, for example, refugee claimants, immigrants who have been declared inadmissible for reasons that cannot be told and illegal immigrants who are struggling to meet the Minister's supposed requirements for admission. It is against this background that I find the section on security provisions against aliens completely unsatisfactory.
I now come to the matter of infiltrators, "agents provocateurs". They have been used plentifully in the past. It is a practice which everyone agrees is unfair and immoral, especially being used by the government of a country against its own citizens who are not even accused of committing a crime. The Keable Commission recommended that this should be done only after a warrant had been issued by a judge. The Pitfield Commission downgraded the idea to guidelines rather than warrants, suggesting something similar to the FBI guidelines in the United States. In fact, it really ought to be necessary and recognized in law that anyone who wishes to carry on this kind of infiltration and disruption should show cause to a judge to justify the warrant and the invasion of privacy. In fact the Solicitor General has ignored the Keable Commission and the Pitfield committee and been completely silent on the matter of ending this practice of infiltration and disruption. We can expect the practices of the 1960s and 1970s with their dirty tricks to continue because the Solicitor General will not oppose them. He had this chance but he will not.
Goodness knows what trouble we may get into if we start digging into the slush fund administered by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts). We may find ourselves up against the Solicitor General for challenging a government program.
February 20, 1984

Finally, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service will not be subject to review by Parliament. The McDonald Commission required a parliamentary committee chosen by the Party Leaders with a right to see all evidence. The Pitfield committee suggested a Security Intelligence Review Committee appointed by the Government with a right to see all evidence and material, rather than a committee of Parliament. The Solicitor General has cut that down to the bone. There will be an appointed committee reflecting government views after consultation with the opposition. This means nothing. They will not be able to see the Cabinet documents that are vital to the operation and are in possession of the service.
Yet this same service can make contracts with unnamed foreign governments or unnamed departments of foreign governments and keep them secret from the Canadian people. Why is this? Has the FBI some dirty work that it wants the Canadian Security Intelligence Service to do, perhaps to help it combat the terrible threat of the American Indians?
The U.S. has more experience in terrorism than Canada. It nevertheless leaves investigation of U.S. citizens suspected of subversion to the FBI. There is oversight of that operation by the Senate and Congress. In Canada our Solicitor General wants to treat Canadians as though we are aliens in our own land, with a civilian force-which is essentially a police force-which will be more answerable to unnamed foreign governments than it will be to the Canadian people through their elected representatives.
The Government ought to withdraw this Bill and bring back a bill which is more in keeping with the recommendations of the McDonald Commission.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great care to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). I certainly found them helpful in explaining why he is strongly opposed to this Bill.
Would he elaborate on one point which he made during the course of his remarks with respect to the vagueness of the mandate which is proposed for the new security service? He referred to the fact that under the provisions of this legislation, groups within Canada who seek to support agencies or individuals in other countries seeking to put an end to oppressive and dictatorial governments may themselves come under surveillance. Could he elaborate on that particular provision of the legislation?

Mr. Speaker, I think it would be useful to draw attention to certain wording in the proposed legislation. A threat to the security of Canada is considered to include, among other things, activities within or relating to Canada directed toward, or in support of, the threat or use of acts of violence against persons or property for the purpose of achieving a political objective within Canada or a foreign state. In other words, anyone in Canada supporting someone in a foreign state who is pursuing a political objective with the use
Security Intelligence Service
of acts of violence may be considered a threat. As I mentioned, the government of South Africa carries out violence against the black people within its borders and in neighbouring states. Therefore, anyone who supports the government of South Africa comes under this category of a threat to the security of Canada. I would think that there are many businessmen, bankers and government servants, for that matter, who come under that category.
Of course, it may be argued that the government will not prosecute those people but only those who are supporting the black people, if they support them by any activity within Canada. In that case the application of the law would be rankly biased and would be completely inconsistent with the actual wording of the law. That is one strong example of the falsity of the wording of this law. It is completely inapplicable to those situations in which Canadians are already engaged.

Mr. Speaker, Clause 17 of the legislation is one provision that I think should be drawn to the attention of the House and those who are following this debate. Perhaps the Member for Spadina might elaborate on this clause which he referred to in the course of his remarks.
According to the provisions of Clause 17(b), the new security service may, following the approval of the Solicitor General and consultations with the Secretary of State for External Affairs:
-enter into an arrangement or otherwise co-operate with the government of a foreign state or an institution thereof or an international organization of states or an institution thereof.
According to this section, as I read it, it would be possible for the new civilian security service to pass on information which it obtains through the use of intrusive techniques. For example, this includes information which it obtains under Clause 16 of this legislation. That information may have nothing whatsoever to do with national security but could be information that would assist Canada in the conduct of its international affairs. It could be information gained from spying on a student group or group of foreign academics who are visiting Canada through opening their mail. In turn, that information could be passed on to an unnamed intelligence agency in a foreign country.
The present Solicitor General has taken the position that he will refuse to tell Canadians the names of the agencies that he is transferring this information to. We have a security agency which is using intrusive techniques to obtain information and pass it on to agencies of other governments, some of which the Solicitor General says are not even acknowledged in their own countries. One can only speculate on what kind of banana republic we are co-operating with when it does not even acknowledge the existence of its own security service. Conceivably those agencies can use that information against relatives or friends of the individuals within Canada. Would the Hon. Member elaborate on his concerns about this particular provision which he referred to in his speech?

February 20, 1984
Security Intelligence Service

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add two points to the very good points made by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). It has already been a long-standing matter of experience that the RCMP passes information to the FBI and that we really have no control of what sort of information is passed. Over the years Canadians who have wanted to enter the United States have been stopped from time to time. There was an incident of a Member of the Order of Canada, a Mrs. Macpherson, who was stopped from entering the United States, perhaps because she was going to a peace rally in New York. This is the kind of intrusion into non-security matters in which the RCMP is engaged and about which it has apparently passed information to the FBI.
Second, there was the disreputable business a few years ago of the kidnapping in Canada of the American Indian leader, Leonard Pelletier, who was returned to the United States in violation of the spirit of the extradition law. In other words, Canadian police officers collaborated with the FBI in a way that violated Canada's security and, incidentally, violated the rights of North America's first people. This is the kind of thing that has been going on and which is now going to be legalized. It will be impossible to criticize it effectively, let alone to bring it to court, if the Solicitor General has his way.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: If there are no further questions, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer) for debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak this morning on Bill C-9. I would urge every Member of this House and all Canadians to recognize that this Bill is of the utmost importance to this country. Many Bills which pass through this House affect our pockets but this Bill affects our liberty. It will continue to affect our liberty as individual Canadians and it will affect our personal lives. In that sense I think we should all be aware of how important it is, when this Bill gets to committee, that each and every Canadian who has an interest be heard. Make no mistake about it, it is very important legislation.
Today we are speaking of the second attempt by this Government to establish a civilian Security Intelligence Service. We are considering the possibility of creating a whole new service, replacing the Royal Canadian Mounted Police security service with one that would have very broad powers indeed to investigate the activities of Canadian citizens.
Let me read the duties and functions of this service in Clause 12 of Bill C-9. This will show how extensive the service is intended to be. Clause 12 reads:
The Service shall collect, by investigation or otherwise, to the extent that it is strictly necessary, and analyse and retain information and intelligence respecting activities that may on reasonable grounds be suspected of constituting threats to the security of Canada and, in relation thereto, shall report to and advise the Government of Canada.
The previous Bill dealing with this matter introduced in this House was Bill C-157. It received a storm of protest from all across the country and from almost every civil rights organization we have, including provincial attorneys general. As the previous speaker said, the Government really achieved a great thing in that all provincial attorneys general agreed to oppose the legislation. That does not happen very often. Police force spokesmen, media commentators and individuals blew up such a storm of protest over the proposed legislation that Bill C-157 was withdrawn.
Then the Government immediately introduced Bill C-9. One wonders why the tremendous hurry to get this legislation into the House. I could not quite understand that until I looked at The Globe and Mail of today's date and found a copy of a story which the Auditor General first revealed. This was the business of the big new office building in Ottawa, the Centennial Towers and its many floors that have been empty for months. Those floors were designed to house this new security commission which we have not yet got and which we might never get, although the Government has already spent over $2 million on empty floor space. If that is not a political boondoggle, I do not know what is. It is not to the credit of the Government that this kind of waste goes on. One wonders, if it takes a 12-storey building or whatever to house a security force that does not exist, what kind of a mammoth organization of super snoopers the Government is trying to impose on Canadians.
The previous Bill was scrutinized carefully by the Senate committee. Some key changes were made in response to the recommendations of that committee. However, not all of the changes which the Senate committee recommended have been included in this Bill. Today is the first time the House of Commons has had an opportunity to debate this matter thoroughly. This debate is the starting point of public scrutiny of what I consider, and of what the Conservative Party considers, most important legislation. We look forward to the time when this Bill goes to committee and every clause is examined in detail and proposed amendments put.
The name of the Bill itself is imposing, startling and frightening. It reads:
An Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to enact An Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereto.
That is an example of the gobbledegook Bill C-9 is filled with which makes it uncertain and unsure what powers this agency will have. The Solicitor General himself has pointed out that this is peculiar and unusual legislation, that most countries do not have their entire security forces under one particular act but leave some parts to the discretion of the respective government. While discretion itself can be a dangerous thing when a sudden shift is made toward full reliance on statutory instruments, it is essential that the statute in question be concisely drafted to ensure it does no more than this Parliament intends it to. In an age when people are increasingly reliant on written documents for the protection of their rights, it is most important the mandate and the powers given to this future organization are clearly limited and unambiguously defined.
February 20, 1984

This new Bill purports to redefine the security intelligence system in Canada. Therefore, we have to ensure it does it correctly. I would like to highlight some, not all, of the concerns I feel are inherent in the provisions of Bill C-9.
The new law aims to deal with people and activities that are considered to be a threat to this country. In particular, the Minister has indicated that the Bill will be directed at controlling the following kinds of activities: classic espionage, sabotage activities, foreign-influenced activities and political violence, such as terrorism and domestic subversion. Certainly these categories are not those we would like to encourage in this country. However, close scrutiny of the provisions of Bill C-9 before us that attempt to cover espionage, foreign-influenced activities, terrorism and domestic subversion, raise some important questions relating to the mandate of the agency. Provision for the review of the activity of the service and the accountability of the agency are also of paramount concern.
Threats to the security of Canada are defined in Clause 2 of the Bill. It reads as follows:
(a)	espionage or sabotage that is against Canada or is detrimental to the interests of Canada or activities directed toward or in support of such espionage or sabotage,
(b)	foreign influenced activities within or relating to Canada that are detrimental to the interests of Canada and are clandestine or deceptive or involve a threat to any person,
(c)	activities within or relating to Canada directed toward or in support of the threat or use of acts of violence against persons or property for the purpose of achieving a political objective within Canada or a foreign state, and
(d)	activities directed toward undermining by covert unlawful acts, or directed toward or intended ultimately to lead to the destruction or overthrow by violence of, the constitutionally established system of government in Canada,-
On the face of it, it seems right and proper that that is what it should do. However, the importance of definitions cannot be overemphasized. The definitions in the Bill are very loose and vague.
The Senate committee reminded us that that section-and this is most important-will establish for the CSIS, its Director and employees, a fundamental standard for their activities. It will enter crucially into judicial determination of whether a particular intrusive technique can be used, and it will provide a benchmark for assessment of agency activities by review bodies and by the agency's political masters, that is, by Parliament. It is very important that the definitions as to what this group of super snoopers can and cannot do are clear and understandable.
I am prepared to admit, as we all are, that the definitions in the new Bill have been tightened significantly, particularly the final paragraph excluding lawful advocacy and protest from the purview of the security service. That is a major improvement. However, the definitions remain too broad in many respects. For example, what do the words "espionage" and "sabotage" mean in the Bill? Surely it is not too difficult and would not restrict the activities of the service to define those terms. It is absolutely essential to define what those words mean.
Security Intelligence Service
Does the inclusion of deceptive activity which is detrimental to the interests of Canada imply that the agency can investigate economic initiatives of foreign countries operating in Canada? On the face of those words, it would certainly seem that those people could investigate, for example, the operations of a Japanese company which is trying to sell its cars. Perhaps this could be construed as being against the interests of Canada. Will our foreign trade now be carried on by a group of super snoopers or secret servicemen? That is a somewhat strange way to run our foreign trade and compete with other countries.
What exactly is contemplated by the phrase "activities within or relating to Canada directed toward or in support of the threat or use of acts of violence against persons or property for the purpose of achieving a political objective within Canada or a foreign state"? A previous speaker mentioned the possibilities which might occur as a result of this clause. We really need to look at these particular sections to ensure that we are not giving this group of secret servicemen, as proposed, too wide a mandate.
Clause 21 of the Bill gives the service extraordinary powers which are to be authorized by a combination of judicial warrant and ministerial approval. Canadians should be aware of what that clause indicates. I would like to repeat part of it because it is very important. In referring to the powers of the agency, Clause 21 (3)(a) reads:
-to enter any place or open or obtain access to any thing;
(b)	to search for, remove or return, or examine, take extracts from or make copies of or record in any other manner the information, record, document or thing; or
(c)	to install, maintain or remove any thing.
Those are very wide powers. They are powers to enter anyone's private property without the person's knowledge. We should be very careful what kind of powers we give this particular group.
The Senate called for a balance between the gravity of the threat to security and personal liberty. That is the key to this whole area. The balance is not here. The Government claims that this balance would be provided by the Minister in accepting or rejecting an application for a warrant, but it does not spell it out specifically. For example, the relationship between the Minister and the Director of the service is not clear. While the Minister plays a direct role in the authorization of warrant applications, the Director is vested with the powers of management and control subject to the direction of the Minister. The key problem with this arrangement is found in Clause 6(2), which provides that the Minister "may" issue written directions. Does this imply that the Minister will have the power to issue oral directions? If he issues oral directions, no record of those directions will come to the attention of the review committee. These are matters on which the Bill is not clear and I say is incomplete.
Finally, let me recite some of my broad concerns about and objections to this Bill. It is my philosophy and view that no legislation should be changed unless there is a demonstrated need and requirement for such legislation; second, unless there
February 20, 1984

Security Intelligence Service
is an urgent and compelling reason to enact new laws. Has such a demonstrated need and a compelling reason been shown? Some may say that two royal commissions have looked at the facts and recommended such a service. On the other hand, facts speak differently to different people. I have not heard to my satisfaction the kinds of facts which would necessitate such an overblown secret service as this Bill proposes. Canada is not a world power. We do not have the requirements of superpowers for secret services. That is part of the entire question we should examine in committee: What is the need for this organization and where has it been shown?
This proposed legislation must of necessity detract from the rights and freedoms of individual Canadians. Civil police forces have a very recent history in the world. The first civil police force was set up in the 1820s. It was the metropolitan police of London, the first in the world. Since that time-and that is not that long ago-every democratic government has had to struggle and experiment with the difficulties in defining the role and limiting the powers of the police so as to not encroach unduly upon civil liberties. It is very difficult to attain that balance. In doing this, the benefit of the doubt must always go to the individual. The balance of freedom must be given to the individual Canadian citizen. It has to be that way. However, that is not so with this piece of legislation, which was designed for the super snoopers themselves. The Minister had a group of potential secret servicemen in his office and they designed the proposed Act so that it fitted their needs.
The first draft, in their own words, was the Rolls-Royce model. It would have taken them quickly to their goal. The second draft, the one before us, they now claim is a Chevrolet or a Ford but will do the job very well. That is the wrong principle. These people should be given what I would call a handyman's wreck or a mechanic's delight-something on which they have to work to make it go. That is essential here. If it does not work, let them return and ask for an amendment to the legislation. It should not be the other way around where the rights and freedoms of Canadians are trampled upon and those Canadians have to come to Parliament and ask that the legislation be amended. That process takes too long and too many rights are trampled upon.
A previous speaker mentioned that the United States has a far greater problem but that its legislation is far tighter. It does not allow freedoms to the super snoopers such as the ones proposed in this legislation. I would like to refer to an article which appeared in the February 11, 1984 edition of The Globe and Mail, which reads in part:
Congressman Donald Edwards, the chairman of the House of Representatives committee which scrutinizes FBI activities, said that the "loose" definitions of threats to national security in the Canadian bill would never be tolerated in the United States.
Mr. Edwards, a liberal democrat from California who once was an FBI agent, said that the Canadian Bill looks like an invitation to trouble. That is exactly what it is. He goes on to say: "We used to let the FBI do these kinds of things, but not
any more." Why should we in this country walk into that kind of trap when we have had the experience with the FBI in the United States? Let us close the door before we open it to make sure that we do not have an Act which allows them to abuse the rights of Canadians.
The record of this Government in respecting the freedom of rights of citizens is anything but good. We do not have to recall very far back in the past when the War Measures Act was passed. That tempest in a teapot took away the rights of all Canadians, rights which had been earned over many years. Thousands of people were jailed in Quebec, but not one was found guilty. They were jailed without a trial, and all had to be let go.
More recently this Parliament passed the elections Bill, I believe it was Bill C-169, which restricted the right of free speech in this country. As the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) said in this House last week, he apologized to his constituents for being part of that. I do the same. It is another example of how, unless you really look at legislation, the government can slip through legislation restricting the rights of people. We have had recent revelations about the PMO and its eagerness to get into the super snooper business. It is an indication of why we should look at this Bill very carefully.
Hundreds of thousands of Canadians have lived under the Russian secret police, the KGB. Hundreds of thousands lived in Nazi Germany and had to deal with the SS. Other hundreds of thousands of Canadians have lived under other dictatorial governments which had a secret service. These people are very concerned. They know that the more dictatorial a government becomes, the greater need such a government has for secret service activities. People in Canada are worried about this legislation, and well they might be. I assure Hon. Members that this Party will oppose this legislation until it is changed to protect the rights of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a couple of questions to the Hon. Member who has just spoken, particularly given the fact that he is the deputy spokesperson for the Ministry of the Solicitor General for his Party. The McDonald Commission strongly recommended the establishment of a committee of Parliament to oversee the operations, in a policy sense and a budgetary sense, of the new civilian security service. Does the Hon. Member support the important recommendation that we not leave the oversight function to the executive, if you will, but rather that there be a parliamentary committee established which would be responsible for overseeing those operations?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree that the key point with regard to this proposed organization is that it should be under the control of Parliament. I believe that suggestion is a good one and should be examined in committee. There may be others, but in my view it is essential that Parliament have final control over this organization.
February 20, 1984
Mr. Speaker, just for clarification, the Hon. Member is supporting the establishment of such a committee to exercise that parliamentary oversight, is he?

Mr. Speaker, that is a good suggestion. I believe that idea will be reviewed in committee. There may be others. If others are better, perhaps that should be the way to go. I confirm my feeling that Parliament should be the final authority and should have control.

Mr. Speaker, following on the answer just given by the Hon. Member, does he feel that Parliament should have access to all material and documents in the possession of the service for the purpose of that review, including all relevant Cabinet documents?

Mr. Speaker, it was the recommendation of the Senate committee that the review committee should have that. I certainly agree with it. There is no reason why the committee should not have access to Cabinet documents dealing with the activities of the secret security service.

Mr. Speaker, the Pitfield committee recommended, and the Government has accepted the recommendation, that the new civilian security service should have sweeping, intrusive powers, including in particular the power to open first-class mail. The Member's colleague from Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) has strongly opposed the recommendation that the security service should have the power to open first-class mail. Can the Hon. Member enlighten the House as to his view whether it is an appropriate function for a civilian security service to be able to open first-class mail? Does he agree with his colleagues from Vancouver South?

Mr. Speaker, my first reaction is no, they should not have the right to open first-class mail; but on the other hand, there may be unusual circumstances which would justify the opening of mail, if there is sufficient evidence. That is a matter that has been left up in the air. There is no evidence before us. Perhaps those who take this position will justify it. Unless they do, I think the position taken by the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) is the right one.

Mr. Speaker, is the Hon. Member in agreement with the McDonald Commission, which would require that if a judge is to be asked to issue a warrant to empower the security service to open first-class mail, one consideration he must weigh is whether the invasion of privacy is outweighed by the indication of danger to national security? That provision was recommended by the McDonald Commission. It is excluded from the Solicitor General's Bill. Is the Hon. Member in favour of having such a provision?

Mr. Speaker, surely the only reason it is taken before a judge is to weigh the balance between private rights and public need. I would approve of the judge doing that. That is all he can do.
Security Intelligence Service

Mr. Speaker, when I first examined the provisions of Bill C-157, the precursor of Bill C-9, it occurred to me that we had an ideal companion piece to the Government's emergency planning order. That order of May, 1981 permitted the same Minister responsible for Bill C-9 to provide for the incarceration of civilian internees and, in the course of such planning, to arrange for the removal of prisoners from penal institutions and to move into those institutions civilian internees.
I questioned the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the House as to the occasion when that emergency planning order might come into effect. It will be recalled that the emergency planning order was divided into two parts. The first part related to circumstances where an emergency had arisen; the second part related to those times where in case of war it was necessary to take these steps. My questions of the Prime Minister, and they are a matter of record in this House, indicated that when I asked him if he would be good enough to restrict the meaning of "war" to include only a situation where a state of war existed between Canada and some foreign nation, he sarcastically responded to me that he supposed I would be interested in hearing about a cold war. A cold war is a state of mind. The mind of the Government will determine whether war exists, if we are to believe what the Prime Minister has said.
Therefore, when I tie in the actions of the Solicitor general of Canada (Mr. Kaplan) under the emergency planning order with the original provisions of Bill C-157 and the residual parts thereof which are included in Bill C-9, I think this is alarming to any Canadian concerned with the security of the person and the civil liberties of Canadians.
If we add to that circumstance of linking those two pieces of legislation the new Bill introduced in the House with respect to amendments to the Criminal Code providing, as it does, for both the seizure and freezing of the property of citizens who are accused of crime without having had benefit of trial, we immediately realize that we have a beautiful triumvirate of legislation. One piece provides for the seizure of the property of the individual before he has ever been convicted on information gathered by a civilian security force which has extraordinary powers under the Bill; and the third prong of the attack against Canadians clearly is the position which would result in their incarceration.
It is alarming that we should be confronted with the type of circumstance that confronts us today. All parliamentarians should be concerned about the departure we have taken from normal practice. I know that if we believe the information provided by the Solicitor General with respect to this Bill, it is only for the purpose of gathering information. The security service will gather information and do nothing else. I rather suspect that when the Gestapo was established, it had no other purpose than to gather information and then implement it.
The great problem is that we have removed from an institution in Canada that is well respected by the citizens of the

February 20, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
country a service which formerly was conducted by them. I know that the RCMP has said that it is not qualified and does not in fact wish to undertake this function. I sometimes wonder whether that assertion is made with regard to the nature of the functions to be undertaken. The RCMP may prefer not to be involved in this type of activity. Something else bothers me about this assertion, Mr. Speaker. I wonder what the real position of the RCMP with respect to the removal of this function from their customary actions may be, in the event that they are able to speak freely and without the pressure of their political bosses being brought to bear upon them. We will never know that, however, as long as this Government holds office.
What is it about the Bill in specific terms that should alarm Canadians? I make a general practice of consulting with my constituents, Mr. Speaker. When Bill C-157 was introduced I communicated with them by way of my regular house-holder mailing, made comments with respect to Bill C-157 and asked a series of questions. One of those questions is as valid today as when I asked it, because the Bill does not remove all of the defects of Bill C-157. That question was: In any revised Security Intelligence Service Bill should members of that service have access to private census and tax information? I realize that census information was removed but tax information was not. Neither were medical records or information contained in a letter that may be deposited with Canada Post.
I am particularly concerned about the effect upon the tax system in Canada in the event that, contrary to the provisions of the Income Tax Act, this Bill overrides the prohibitions against disclosure by members and employees of Revenue Canada to the security service. One of the fundamental tenets of proper tax disclosure in a self-assessing system is the recognition by the taxpayer that what he or she reports is confidential and will be used only for the purpose of assessing tax. There may well be circumstances where, in obeying the tax laws of Canada, people may have breached other laws. I say quite frankly that if you wish the tax system of self-assessment to be maintained as the cornestone of our taxing arrangements, then it is absolutely vital that that information supplied by taxpayers be confidential and used only for the purpose of assessing tax.
This Bill will go a long way toward shattering the confidence-if any is left-that taxpayers have in the system administered by the Government. I do not know if the general public is fully aware of the implications of the Bill on their tax reporting system, but they certainly will be by the time we are finished with it in the House. We have an obligation to disclose to Canadians exactly what the Government is doing to them. Because we have raised issues in the House which have been elaborated upon and followed very closely by the media, we already know that the general public is aware of the ill deeds perpetrated upon the taxpayers of Canada by the Government. We can only hope that we can rectify the damage done to the system by the Government's actions.
However, if the House, in reckless fashion, passes Bill C-9 without regard to the damage it will do to the tax system, then
when this Party forms the Government it will have a very difficult task trying to convince the people of Canada that it is appropriate that they honestly and fairly report all sources of income.
There is one other matter that concerns me about this legislation, Mr. Speaker. While we know that the mails are used for the purpose of transmitting drugs and other contraband products, it is my belief that the sanctity that has attached to letters being part of first-class mail ought to be maintained. A letter is but a written communication, with nothing else in the envelope. Indeed, first-class mail may include not only letters but the contents of an envelope in addition to the written material. That may well include contraband material, drug substances and the like. While it may be appropriate to examine a written communication that has attached or included with it contraband material, I submit it is not appropriate to open letters being part of first class mail. That matter has not been dealt with by the legislation. As a matter of fact, the Bill would entitle those pursuing the duties outlined for them in the Bill to open all mail, including letters in Canada, as it appealed to them.
One of the great defects that existed in Bill C-157 was clearly the lack of responsibility to the House by any minister of government who, whether he believed it or not, was responsible for the actions of this service. Thank heavens that has been remedied. It is a sad reflection upon the attitude of government that it would even contemplate the introduction of a Bill that tried to remove responsibilities from a minister of the Crown who was answerable in the House for the actions of a department of government or agency for which he should have assumed responsibility.
As a matter of fact, as I look at "intention", it worries me, Mr. Speaker, to find that any government would have had the audacity to attack the civil liberties of Canadians in the fashion of this Government when it introduced Bill C-157. To remove part of those offensive provisions does not, to my mind, eliminate the scorn which should be heaped on a Government which is so inclined to attack with reckless abandon the freedoms we enjoy in Canada. It so happens, of course, that it is the same Government which made much ado about a Charter of Rights and Freedoms which it attacks and assaults at every opportunity.
I am concerned about the search warrant provisions. We know that, as a general rule, mechanical functioning of oft changed provisions is left to the Governor in Council. The reason for that is that Parliament surely cannot be responsible on a daily basis for the minute changes which must be made in order to make a piece of legislation function smoothly. However, I am submitting to the House that consequent upon the delegation by Parliament to the Governor in Council under Clause 28 to pass those regulations dealing with such significant matters as warrants, is an unacceptable deletation by Parliament, and I quote from Clause 28-"governing the practice and procedure of, and security requirements appli-
February 20, 1984

cable to, hearings of applications for such warrants and for renewals of such warrants", we should know, Mr. Speaker, what the requirements ought to be. Is it a simple necessity under the intended plans of the Government that an application without more be submitted? I think not. Parliament should surely be aware of the very strict rules which should apply when the security of Canada is in jeopardy.
I wonder whether, having created a new force outside the ambit of the RCMP-which is not under the control and responsibility of the Solicitor General-we do not need some general principles which should apply with respect to those circumstances which would entitle members of the force to obtain those search warrants, which, as I indicated earlier, extend so far as to permit encroachment on the tax system, medical records and letters dispatched in the mail?
We have been told by the Government that this Bill meets one additional substantial complaint which was raised by the Senate committee which examined Bill C-157. That is that once an application has been made for a search warrant and has been turned down, the applicant cannot shop for a judge who will be more amenable to the desires of the person making the application. This Bill, Mr. Speaker, does not in fact preclude shopping for judges. All it requires is that some note be made of the fact that another judge may have accepted or rejected an application. If, indeed, the Government wishes to put an end to shopping for judges who would be more amenable to the requirements, all it needs to do is provide that once an application has been made to the court, another application may not be made for the same kind of search warrant. If the Government has the courage to do that, and I invite it to do so, we will have evidence of its alleged good intentions. If it, indeed, means what it says, let that change be made so that this Bill will remove that ominious provision which exists.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Hon. Member if he could comment further on the matter of Revenue Canada and confidentiality. If a person has been contributing to some organizations, perhaps a church organization or a public group which is supporting liberation movements in South Africa or in Central America, and if it were found through this kind of intrusive mail opening that the individual had applied for a tax exemption in the case of an organization which had that exemption available to it, would the Hon. Member feel that that would be an improper use of this kind of intrusion?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is asking me a question of law as to whether or not, as a consequence of making a donation to a charitable organization so recognized, the status of the charitable organization might be removed for some other purpose. That has nothing to do with this Bill, as I see it. My objection to this legislation is-and I thought I dealt with it rather extensively-that I did not want that information to fall into the hands of persons other than those entitled to receive it for simple tax purposes. I thought the requirement was rather clear that only for the purposes of assessing tax should anyone examine information in a tax return.
Security Intelligence Service
This Bill, as the Hon. Member knows, in fact breaches that general provision of the Income Tax Act as it presently exists. I believe I have rather clearly indicated that, to my mind, this has a detrimental effect, not only upon the rights of the citizen who filed the information, but has a further detrimental effect upon the whole self-assessment process.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his answer which does succintly clarify his intention on that point. I would ask him as well, apart from the income tax side of it, whether he considers it appropriate that under this Bill, if it is adopted, the security service could choose to investigate by intrusive methods, such as mail opening, people who support, for example, the campaign in Africa against apartheid.

Mr. Speaker, I do not believe it is appropriate, as I have indicated, to examine for any purpose letters sent by any person, including those who might have made a political contribution to sustain the democratic government of El Salvador.
Mr. Speaker, as is rarely the case, perhaps I should say with respect to the Hon. Member, I certainly share many of the concerns he has expressed this morning and his philosophical approach.
John, you are in trouble now.

On the question of access to information, I certainly agree with the Hon. Member that information should be held in confidence and should be used for the purpose for which it was intended. I would like the Hon. Member to elaborate on this particular point. The Hon. Member indicated clearly that it is his view that the new security intelligence agency should not have the power to open first-class mail in the absence of some suggestion that it contains some contraband, I suppose. I would like to ask the Hon. Member whether, in addition to precluding access by the security intelligence agency to records of the Department of National Revenue, he would extend that to other records which are obtained by other federal Departments, such as family allowance records, records which are obtained as a result of an application for unemployment insurance benefits and records which are obtained by the Federal Business Development Bank. Would he preclude the new security intelligence agency from having access to those records as well?

Mr. Speaker, I identified two areas which I thought were matters of immediate concern. I based my attack upon the opening or gathering of information related to those two issues on the basis of either well established, recognized law in the general domain or statute law. What I am saying is that today it is an offence to disclose information to persons other than those entitled to use that information for the purpose of assessing tax. That would be a change in the statute law.
We recognize in Canada that treating letters in the mail as private communications has been sacrosanct. The Hon. Member asked me whether I would go beyond that and my

February 20, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
answer has to be this. I have not compiled, as he probably has, a list of a variety of information which would be available under this Bill but is not now available. I ask him: Is it not available because of the statute law or because of a well recognized principle known to all Canadians which ought not to be changed? If it is because of either of those two circumstances that the information cannot now be made available to the security service, then I would say it should not further be made available.

I thank the Hon. Member for his answer. In fact, as the McDonald Commission clearly documented, it is as a result of present statutory prohibitions that this information cannot be made available. I take it that the Hon. Member would continue those statutory prohibitions. He is indicating his agreement.
I would like to ask him to elaborate on the results of the householder questionnaire circulated in his constituency. He touched briefly on that. Given the fact the Hon. Member made the effort to seek the views of his constituents on this important matter, then perhaps he might go into the outcome of that questionnaire at some greater length.

Mr. Speaker, I would be delighted. I should have referred to it when I brought it up initially. The result of my tabulation is that my constituents opposed, by a ratio of two to one, making available to the service tax information and census material. It is true this Bill precludes the service from gaining census information. Accordingly, I suppose the result is somewhat coloured. I did not break it down in the questionnaire and ask if they were opposed to tax information and were they opposed to census information. They simply expressed the view of being opposed to both.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the results because we have not heard from any Liberal Members except the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary on this legislation. It seems they are not too keen to defend the principle of this Bill.
Does the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Gamble) believe that the new civilian security service should have the power to place under surveillance-setting aside the question of opening mail and access to Government records-groups in Canada which seek to support the African National Congress campaign in South Africa against apartheid? Does he believe they should be placed under surveillance or that the security service should have the power to place such groups under surveillance in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, it would depend indeed upon the circumstances involved in the activity of any representative of that group in this country. We know there are laws in Canada-I refer to the Immigration Act-which establish a number of prohibited classes of visitors to Canada. If they have come to Canada for the purpose of advocating the overthrow of a foreign government, they indeed would be, in my view, properly subject today to an examination and surveillance process instituted by the RCMP. Very clearly, then, if the RCMP can do it today, I would have no objection, having regard to the specific provisions of the Immigration Act which have some validity, to the security service doing the same kind of work in the future.

Mr. Speaker, this subject matter has long been under consideration in this country. As far as this House is concerned, I suppose the problems of security were discovered when the McDonald Commission came into being. However, I can recall the decision to establish the security service under the RCMP with a civilian director. First, if I recall, it was General Dare and subsequently John Starnes.
The other way around.

My colleague says it was the other way around and I stand corrected. But it goes a long way back. I think there is great confusion in the public mind, which is usually the result of a momentary glance at news headlines or some quick report on television; but there is no doubt in my mind that Canada needs a security agency. To say it is an intelligence gathering agency is to immediately stamp it, as those civil libertarians who want utter licence to prevail at all times would do, with the label of a government snoop agency burrowing into the innermost secrets of all Canadians for whatever purpose the active imagination may wish to bring forth.
Our history, Mr. Speaker, since World War II has been a joke in so far as security is concerned. Foreign governments have sent agents into this country to operate not necessarily against Canada but as a convenient base to operate against the United States. We became aware of this through the Gouzenko disclosures. But the country involved in that case, the Soviet Union, is not the only one to carry on nefarious activities in this country.
In every major security contest there has ever been, Canada has come out second simply because we did not have the resources or the determination to do something about it. I find it rather amusing that people are concerned about opening mail to see whether one supports apartheid or not, some church group or this or that. That is a silly froth on the subject. In so far as National Revenue is concerned, it opens mail; of course it does and it has a right to. It does not require a civilian agency to go and get a court order. I can see some people shaking their heads. They have never faced the problem of heroin importation by letter. It can be done and very simply. They have not faced the smuggling of almost pure gold in fine chains in a thick letter. They have not seen the absolute pornographic filth which comes in via the mail. It is not only mail; there are visual demonstrations of some of the most violent filth you can imagine. Perhaps some of the people who object to this privately enjoy viewing these, I do not know. 1 rather suspect that many of those who protest in print and otherwise protest too much. On the customs side it is not necessary. The authority is there. Under the Post Office Act it is rather stupid. The inspectors of the postal service have the
February 20, 1984

right to examine mail to see if it contains contraband. When they find contraband they write a letter to the addressee telling him there is a parcel for him coming from somewhere and to come and get it. Of course, the addressee is not going to go anywhere near the Post Office. They are then under instruction to return it to the sender. Of all the stupid things to do. I can only categorize that as stupid. That is an attempt to suborn legitimate law in the country. I defy any civil libertarian to say it is wrong to use means such as the censorship of mail by the appropriate officials to prevent the entry into Canada of narcotics and other attempts at smuggling.
In regard to the Income Tax Act, I agree that it has gone too far. I object to the agreement that was signed secretly between the RCMP and the Department of National Revenue and not disclosed until an admission was pulled from the lips of the then Minister, now Senator Guay, some years ago that it was possible for the RCMP to examine income tax files in an investigation of an offence under the Income Tax Act. The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) knows this. Right away both the RCMP and the Department of National Revenue breached that agreement by doing something quite contrary to it.
This is precisely what many of the critics or potential critics of this Act are saying. In a criminal prosecution the income tax files of certain individuals were examined by the RCMP. The Anderson case is an example of that. That is wrong. The sooner the Solicitor General and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) come clean as to the exact status of that agreement today and its strict adherence, the better off we will be.
That is why I agree with my colleague from Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn). This Act requires full examination by a committee of the House. We have seen security examined by the other place, by royal commissions and God knows what. The House of Commons, which is deemed by the people of Canada to represent them, must be able to get the views of a lot of people from one end of the country to the other. It is not sufficient for lobby groups and persons concentrated around Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto to give us the benefit of their views. A few of them give their views by way of briefs. Many of them give their views by reports of speeches, which are synthesized versions of what is said depending upon the views of the reporter.
I underline the absolute necessity, Mr. Speaker, when this legislation goes to committee, that the committee, composed of all Members of the House, shall then have an opportunity to go from Victoria to St. John's and hear what the people of Canada have to say about the important issue of a security agency for the country. By that I mean the relationship to government of what has to be a vital agency concerning individuals. We are attempting to protect the security of the country not only from boring in from the outside, but from activities within the country which include violent means,
Security Intelligence Service
uprisings and a variety of other illegal ways to overthrow government and create national confusion.
Having said that, I do not want to come down hard on either side. I would personally tend to favour a civilian agency with a director with much more responsibility to the Minister than is required under this Act. Mr. Speaker, one of the big problems we have had in the past 20 years is that the Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has not been responsible directly to the Minister; he has been made responsible to a Deputy Minister. I will admit that over the years the history of the Department of the Solicitor General has been somewhat unhappy in that, along with a few other ministries, it was one of the favourite stools in the game of ministerial musical chairs. The net result was that either new boys to Cabinet or people who could not do a job properly in a more senior position were allotted to the position of Solicitor General. Subordination to the Deputy Solicitor General and the nature of leadership did much to affect the morale all the way through the force.
Therefore I disagree with Clause 7 of the Bill which stipulates that the Director should consult the Deputy Minister about the general operational policies of the service. I suggest that that is nonsense. He is responsible to the Minister because there must be proper political direction. That clause merely reflects part of the mandarin desire to control everything here in Ottawa.
I agree with Clause 8 of the Bill. A service that is properly run by a good Director should choose its own people. The service's employees should not necessarily be tall, blonde and 22. They would meet the requirements of the RCMP and make excellent policemen. A security service should be made up of its own full-time employees rather than people who are seconded through a backdoor from another government agency. Those who work with a security agency must possess the best possible qualifications. Their qualifications include intelligence, language and many other factors but have very little to do with being trained for a national police force. The security service should not become an independent force with the power of arrest. I personally believe that that is the purpose of the RCMP and other police forces. Any suggestion that the security agency should be allowed to arrest people or take other police action which people may fear should be set aside at the beginning.
I have some personal knowledge about the attraction of the RCMP as a career for young men and women in this country. All of the offences laid against the RCMP as a result of the McDonald Commission related to security. The besmirching of the RCMP has discouraged many good recruits from joining that force. I will admit that present economic conditions do not allow for many vacancies and we read reports about the emptiness of the Regina police school. However, that is not the whole story.
Since my time is almost up, I would suggest to Hon. Members, even those who believe a central security agency or

February 20, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
even the RCMP are inherently bad because they often restrict the aspired licence of some individuals in this country, that I believe the majority of people in this country are in favour of an appropriate security agency. However, since we have not heard what all of the features of that agency should be, I agree with my colleague from Saskatoon that the committee should be given the authority to conduct hearings in all parts of Canada and report back when it has completed its work.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member indicated that he felt the new civilian security service should have certain powers to open first-class mail, particularly when there is a suspicion that there might be contraband in that mail. Does he agree with the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Gamble) that the security service should not in fact have the power to open first-class mail when there is a suspicion that this mail may contain messages of a subversive nature? Does he believe that a distinction should be made between the suspicion of physical contraband being in a first-class envelope and the passing of messages, as his colleague for North York does, or does he believe that all first-class mail should be subject to opening by the new civilian security service?

First, may I say that the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) must have been looking at something else because I did not say that this agency should have the right to open correspondence or parcels with regard to contraband. There already are ample provisions within the Department of National Revenue, customs and excise and the post office for that purpose.
With respect to the suspicion of subversive messages, I find it difficult to answer that because there are pros and cons to the issue. Let us take a case in which correspondence contains codes and the results of espionage. Let us say that espionage is being carried out in the United States by another country and that a post office box in Canada is being used as a marshalling point for the transmission of such information. Surely if it became known to the security agency that this means was being used, would it not be proper for the agency to apply to a court to allow mail being delivered to a particular address to be subject to scrutiny? 1 am talking about national security. I can think of dozens of ways in which our country can be seen as the softest touch in the world for those engaged in international espionage.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member also dealt in his remarks with the question of the mandate of the new security service. He went to some length dealing with the powers that it might possess. Would he expand upon his views with respect to the mandate of the new security service? Of course, having read the legislation carefully, he is no doubt aware of what could happen to a group in his constituency under the provisions of this Bill. Take the example of a church group in Edmonton that decides it wants to send funds or other material assistance to a movement in Central America which is engaged in an attempt to overthrow one of the dictatorial, oppressive and violent governments there so as to liberate people from decades of economic and social oppression. A
Canadian group or individual who wants to support that particular organization would be subject to intrusive techniques being used against it or him, even though many of us would argue that this poses no threat whatsoever to the security of Canada and Canadians. I hear the Hon. Member from Mississauga suggesting it does. I would welcome the intervention of the Member from Mississauga in this debate on that point.
At this juncture in the debate I would like to ask the Hon. Member from Edmonton whether he shares the view of his colleague from Mississauga that such activities by Canadians in fact constitute a threat to the security of Canada and should subject those Canadians to the full range of intrusive powers available to the nearest new security service under the provisions of this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, on the simple basis which the Hon. Member puts it forth, there is no threat to Canada within or even without. If a Canadian citizen feels he wants to send money to a particular group in a particular country, it is that person's business. But I will say this much. If he sends it to a church group that enjoys the status of a charitable organization under the Income Tax Act, 1 would say right away that that organization should be disqualified because it is not carrying on charitable or religious work in the accepted sense. It is carrying on political work in some other country and that is not within the ambit of the Income Tax Act. Therefore, a choice will have to be made. As a matter of fact, some of the so-called charitable organizations front for activities outside the country which are not charitable. The Hon. Member being a man well versed in the law, I would invite him to review the legislation and the court cases with regard to what is the meaning of "charity" in the legal sense. It is not "benevolent" or "useful" but charitable within the meaning of the Act. Then that will follow.
But let us go on and develop the theme beyond what the Hon. Member suggested. He set a simplistic problem. I do not want my answer to be taken as a simplistic approval of a much bigger thesis, because there may be a point of halt. May I say that I would certainly have legislation available-and this may be something we may have to consider here-that in the event hostility should break out involving Canada, or a serious threat of hostility, all of this goes by the board. Many of these safeguards have to go by the board. The Hon. Member is too young to have gone through World War II. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that so many of the things that he and some of his colleagues seem to want and insist upon-I do not know, but I suppose acquired rights-in wartime just do not exist. The national will says that the thing to do is survive, and that has to be understood.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The period for questions has ended.
February 20, 1984
Mr. Speaker, 1 would be willing to commence my remarks now or call it one o'clock, depending upon the will of the House.
No, it is 12.55 p.m.

I am happy to speak to Bill C-9 and to address the three basic questions that are in the Bill. First is a proposed mandate to set up a new civilian service in Canada for the purpose of intelligence operations. Second is to look at the powers that it is suggested the service will have. Third is to look at the oversight and accountability mechanisms that would be established in the Bill or that are established there now to see that the Bill functions and that the service is given limits of operation.
I want to address the Bill from a philosophical point of view. I would also like to use some of my experience, having lived in countries where intelligence services had a very high profile. I felt that instead of bringing security to people, it brought great insecurity.
I do believe this Bill and its notion is one that has grave concerns for many Canadians. I have addressed various audiences on the background notion of what is taking place in the Bill being proposed. I think it is important, to begin with, to look at the word "security". I personally believe its English context has changed in the last 15 years. When I was younger, security, I believe, meant a state of well-being that one experienced because of a whole variety of conditions that were present at that time in the person's life. Today security, 1 believe, means a process by which you guard something or set up walls against insecurity.
Let me outline a case in point. This House of Commons until recently did not have a security system. People coming to sit and watch in the galleries did not have to pass a screening to come into the galleries. People now have to go through mechanical surveillance similar to those installed at airports. However, I feel no more secure in this House of Commons from some attack against my person. In fact, I feel less secure than before.
The question has been thrown into the minds of many people, are we secure here? We had an incident a few weeks ago. A person came to the door at the end of the morning session. Our caucus was sitting here. The person tried to get in. The guards, the security people, whoever, took the person away. During Question Period the same afternoon the same person appeared at the door upstairs and had in her hand a bundle which she threw into the centre of the House of Commons. The proceedings carried on. I am sure many people watching television did not know anything had happened. It turned out the bundle was not a dangerous weapon or anything of the sort, but if it had been, that person had actually passed through security and had put us all into great insecurity.
1 have watched this process grow. I have seen how people put a wall around something to make it secure. Then someone Finds a hole in the wall and one then has to erect another wall. A place where this wall building has taken place is the airport
at Tel Aviv, Israel. Wall after wall after wall have been put up to accommodate this word security.
I see it is one o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I will continue to address the philosophical notion behind security after the lunch hour.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of the House the fact that achievements in any walk of life are a result of team effort. No man or woman achieves greatness by himself or herself, especially in an Olympic sport where it takes a complete effort by a dedicated coach who believes in the ability of his athlete, the support and encouragement of team-mates who know the individual has the "right stuff' to conquer the world, the love and encouragement of parents and relatives who know the hard work required to produce an Olympic medal athlete, and the proud support of the community which recognizes one of its own who brings honour to the community.
Those ingredients were all there last week, but they would not have come together without a supreme, championship effort by one individual, a true world champion. I ask the House to recognize the athlete himself, silver medal winner, men's figure skating champion, 1984 Olympics, from the riding of Simcoe North, Brian Orser.
Hear, hear!

FRANCO-MANITOBANS' RIGHTS POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the weekend, the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party tried once again to obscure the issue of French rights in Manitoba when he stated that his Party's dissenting Members had decided officially to toe the Party line. The Leader of the

February 20, 1984
Opposition forgot to tell the whole truth, however. First, this is not the first time the Members for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) and Simcoe-South (Mr. Stewart) have spoken out against bilingualism in Canada, and the token statement made by one of the Members sounds like a strategic ploy.
